lessons.title: Life Processes: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Living things grow, take in nutrients, breathe, reproduce, remove waste, respond to their surroundings and finally die. Plants get energy from light through photosynthesis, while animals get energy from the food they eat.

Characteristics of Living Things

The basic characteristics of living things are growth, nutrition, respiration, sensitivity, reproduction and excretion. Plants and animals both show these life processes, with some similarities and differences between them.

Living and Non-Living Things

Living things grow in size, take in food for energy, breathe, respond to changes around them, reproduce their own kind and remove waste from their bodies. Non-living things do none of these: they do not grow, eat, breathe, respond or reproduce.

Respiration

During respiration, a living body exchanges gases with its surroundings to obtain energy from food. Animals take in oxygen from the air and release carbon dioxide. Plants take in carbon dioxide in daytime and release oxygen, and at night they take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide.

Sensitivity

Sensitivity is the ability of living things to detect and respond to changes in their environment. Plants grow towards light, the leaves of the mimosa plant close when touched, and we blink when bright light shines into our eyes.

Habitat

A habitat is a place where a plant or an animal lives, such as a forest for many plants, birds, insects and animals. A habitat provides everything a living organism needs, including food, water and space, and helps it to grow, reproduce and increase its population.

How Plants and Animals Reproduce

Plants mostly produce flowers, in which fruits and seeds develop. When seeds mature, they are dispersed by wind, insects and animals, and under favourable conditions they germinate and grow into seedlings.

In animals, reproduction happens in two ways: some females, like birds, fish, lizards and snakes, lay eggs which hatch after a set time, while others, like goats, cats, cows and humans, give birth to their young ones.

Light and Nutrients for Plant Growth

Light is essential because plants use sunlight to prepare their own food by photosynthesis, and the food gives them energy for growth and other activities. Plants grown in bright light are taller and healthier than plants kept in the dark.

Nutrients are equally important: plants absorb nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, along with minerals like calcium, magnesium and iron, from the soil through their roots, and these nutrients keep plants healthy and growing.

lessons.title: Plant Structure and Function: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Plants are classified into flowering and non-flowering plants. A flowering plant has roots, stem, leaves, flowers and fruits, and each part has its own function. Flowers carry out pollination, fruit and seed formation.

Flowering Plants

Flowering plants include wheat, rice, corn, roses, sunflower, tomato, watermelon and grapes. Most plants on Earth today are flowering plants, and they produce flowers, then fruits which contain seeds.

How Non-Flowering Plants Reproduce

Non-flowering plants do not produce flowers or fruits. Mosses and ferns reproduce through spores, which are single-celled reproductive units dispersed by wind or water that develop into new plants. Conifers such as Quetta pine, juniper and chalgoza pine produce seeds inside cones.

Transport of Water in Plants

Plants absorb water through their roots: tiny root hairs absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil, the roots transport the water upward into the stem, and the stem moves it through small tubes to the leaves and other parts of the plant.

Parts of a Carpel

The three parts of a carpel are the stigma, the style and the ovary. The stigma is the upper part which receives pollen, the style is the long tube-like structure connecting the stigma to the ovary, and the ovary is the enlarged basal part which contains the ovules.

Function of Stamens

Stamens are the male reproductive part of a flower. Each stamen has an anther, the swollen top part where pollen grains containing male reproductive cells are formed, and a filament, the long thread-like structure that supports the anther, supplies it with water and nutrients, and helps in pollination.

Life Cycle of a Flowering Plant

A life cycle is the series of changes that a plant goes through during its life. A flowering plant starts from a seed, which germinates under favourable conditions of water, air and suitable temperature into a seedling. The seedling grows into a mature plant, which produces flowers, then fruits and seeds, and the mature seeds are dispersed so that a new life cycle begins again.

Draw the cycle in order: seed, germination, seedling, mature plant with flowers, fruit, seeds, and dispersal back to a new seed.

People Who Work with Plants

A botanist studies plants, including their structure, function, reproduction, growth and uses. A farmer cultivates crops and looks after them, using tools and equipment for sowing, growing and harvesting, and also raises animals and looks after their health.

A florist sells flowers and makes flower designs such as bouquets and wreaths, ensuring a supply of fresh flowers for weddings and other occasions. A gardener cultivates plants of interest on a small scale, improves landscapes by planting trees and flowers, and maintains lawns and controls weeds.

lessons.title: Animal Structure and Function: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Animals are classified into vertebrates, which have a backbone, and invertebrates, which do not. Vertebrates fall into five classes: fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

Vertebrates and Invertebrates

Vertebrates are animals that have a backbone in their body and a skeleton inside their body, for example fish, frog, lizard, pigeon, dog, cat and humans. Invertebrates are animals without a backbone, for example insects, spiders, worms, snails and jellyfish. Most animals on Earth are invertebrates.

Five Classes of Vertebrates

The five classes of vertebrates are fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

How Fish Breathe

Fish breathe through gills. The gills absorb oxygen from the water, so fish can live and swim in water using their tail and fins.

Reptiles

Five reptiles are lizard, snake, tortoise, crocodile and sea turtle. Reptiles have dry, scaly skin and a backbone. Most live on land and lay eggs, and snakes have no legs and crawl on their abdomen.

Jellyfish

A jellyfish is not a true fish because it does not have a backbone. It is an invertebrate with a jelly-like body and tentacles, found in the ocean, while true fishes are vertebrates with a backbone, fins and gills.

Fishes and Amphibians

Fishes live in water, have a tail and fins which help them in swimming, breathe through gills that absorb oxygen from the water, and lay eggs in water. Salmon, goldfish, rohu and shark are examples.

Amphibians live on land but reproduce in water: frogs, toads and salamanders lay eggs in water, the larva comes out of each egg and breathes through gills like a fish, and when it becomes adult it breathes through lungs and skin and has four legs for moving on land.

Preventing Tooth Decay and Gum Disease

Tooth decay is caused when bacteria in the mouth produce acid which breaks down the enamel, the outer protective covering of teeth, making holes or cavities. Gum diseases are also caused by bacteria, and infected gums become red, swollen and may bleed.

To prevent them: brush your teeth regularly at least twice a day, eat a healthy and balanced diet, avoid eating too many chocolates, candies and soda drinks, remove food particles and plaque on a daily basis, and have a regular dental examination so that problems are detected early.

lessons.title: Ecosystem and Adaptations: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
An ecosystem is made of living and non-living things in a place, and living things adapt to their surroundings: fish to water, birds to air, cactus to deserts, and pine and deodar to cold places.

Ecosystem

An ecosystem is an area where living and non-living things interact with each other. Forests, ponds, rivers, grasslands and deserts are all different types of ecosystems.

Forest and Grassland

A forest is a large area with many trees, along with many small plants and animals like birds, insects, reptiles and mammals. A grassland has many different types of grasses but very few trees, and animals like deer, elephant, zebra, lions and birds are found there.

Hibernation

Hibernation, also known as winter sleep, is a survival strategy in which many animals become inactive during winter to conserve energy when there is a lack of food and water. They slow down their heart beat rate and breathing and use stored fat as a source of energy. Frogs, snakes, bats and bears hibernate during winter.

Camouflage

Animals camouflage, that is, they blend in with their surroundings, so that they are less visible to their predators and can survive better. The green colour of grasshoppers makes them less visible in the leaves of plants, chameleons change colour to match their surroundings, and the white fur of a polar bear helps it blend in with snow and ice.

Plants and Animals of the Desert

Desert plants include cactus, which stores water in its small thick leaves and fleshy stem. Desert animals include camels, lizards, snakes and scorpions. Deserts get very little rain each year and have very few plants because of lack of water and high temperature.

Responses to Environmental Conditions

All living things detect changes in their environment and respond to them, and these responses help them to find food, avoid danger and adapt to changing conditions. Any detectable change in the environment is called a stimulus, for example light, temperature, sound, taste, smell and touch.

Plants grow towards sunlight and a sunflower turns its head to face the sun, birds migrate to avoid cold winters, a frog hibernates in winter, we blink in response to sharp light, and a dog salivates at the smell of food.

Population Growth, Urbanization and Habitats

Human population is increasing rapidly, and with it the need for food, water, clothing and housing has increased, so more roads, buildings, dams and vehicles are being built. Factories and vehicles burning fossil fuels cause pollution, all of which harm the habitats of living things.

Urbanization, the movement of population from rural areas towards cities for better health, education and employment, expands cities and destroys natural habitats like forests and wetlands, causing loss of habitats, overcrowding, lack of sanitation and drinking water, and air pollution. When a habitat changes, the organisms living in it are affected too: cutting trees on a large scale causes deforestation, animals lose food and shelter, and are compelled to migrate or die and may become extinct forever.

lessons.title: Matter and its Characteristics: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space, and it exists in three states: solid, liquid and gas. Metals are shiny, strong conductors of heat and electricity, while insulators do not allow electricity to pass through them.

Three States of Matter

The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. A solid has a definite shape and volume, a liquid has a definite volume but no definite shape of its own, and a gas has neither a definite shape nor a definite volume.

StateShape and Volume
SolidDefinite shape and definite volume
LiquidDefinite volume but no definite shape
GasNo definite shape and no definite volume

Solids and Liquids

Solids are hard, do not easily bend or change their shape, and have a definite shape and volume because their particles are very close together and tightly packed. Solids cannot flow because their particles only vibrate around fixed positions.

Liquids have a definite volume but no fixed shape: they take the shape of their container and can flow because their particles can move from one place to another, and their particle arrangement is not fixed.

Volume

Volume is the amount of space occupied by an object, and it deals with the length, width and height of an object. The unit of volume is cubic meter (m3), and volume is calculated as Length x Width x Height.

Floating, Sinking and Density

Floating or sinking depends upon density. A metal needle sinks in water because its density is higher than water. Objects float when they have less density than water, like ice cubes, and sink when they have higher density than water, like coins.

Processes Associated with Heating

Heating is associated with melting and boiling: melting is the process by which a solid changes to a liquid state on heating, and boiling is the process by which a liquid changes into a gaseous state when it is heated. Further heating can vapourize a liquid into a gas. The melting point of ice is 0 degrees C and the boiling point of pure water is 100 degrees C.

Characteristics of Gases

Gases do not have a definite shape and volume: they occupy all available space and take the shape of their container, and their particles move freely in all directions. Gases can be easily compressed because there are a lot of empty spaces between their molecules. Examples of gases include nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and the air surrounding the Earth is a mixture of different gases.

Properties of Metals

Metals are elements which are shiny and good conductors of heat and electricity. Metals like gold, silver and copper have a shiny appearance and are widely used in jewellery making. The texture of metals may be smooth, rough, soft, hard or bumpy, and most metals have a silvery-grey colour, though gold is deep yellow and copper is red-orange.

Different metals have different densities: aluminium is a light metal with low density used in laptops and mobile phones, while iron is a heavy metal with high density used in buildings. Metals like silver, copper, stainless steel, iron and aluminium are good conductors of heat and electricity, so they are used in cooking utensils and in electrical wiring.

chapters.title: Unit 6: Forms of Energy and Energy Transfer

lessons.title: Forms of Energy: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Energy is the ability to do work, and it appears as light, sound, heat, electrical and magnetic energy. Light travels in a straight line, sound is produced by vibrations, and heat is measured by a thermometer.

Energy

Energy is defined as the ability of a body to do work, and we need energy to perform our daily works. Light energy allows us to see objects around us, and sound energy makes us able to hear through our ears.

How Sound is Produced

Sound is produced when the source vibrates: the only cause to produce sound is vibration, the back and forth motion of an object. When you pluck a guitar string it vibrates and makes sound, when you clap your hands your palms hit each other and vibrate, and when we talk the vocal cords in our throat vibrate to produce sound.

Soft and Loud Sound

A sound is soft when the vibrations that make it are very gentle and carry less energy, and it produces a pleasant effect on the ears, for example whispering and chirping of birds. A sound is loud when the vibrations produced by it are very strong, and it may leave an unpleasant effect on our ears, for example the horn of a big truck, thundering and shouting.

Natural and Artificial Sources of Light

Natural sources of light are those not made by humans: the Sun is the main natural source of light, and stars, lightning and fireflies are other natural sources. Artificial sources of light are those created by humans, and they include lantern, street light, LED lights, tube light, candle and torch.

Magnetic Energy

Magnetic energy is the energy of magnets that attracts other magnets and magnetic materials.

Light Energy and Its Properties

Light energy is a form of energy that allows us to see various objects around us. The Sun is the main natural source of light energy, and plants prepare their food in the presence of sunlight.

Light travels in a straight line, known as a light ray, and it does not bend or twist around but goes straight ahead unless something blocks it or changes its path. Light spreads out in all directions with very high speed, and the speed of light in vacuum or air is faster than any other thing, so light from the Sun reaches Earth in about 8 minutes 20 seconds. When light hits an object it bounces back, which is called reflection of light, while a shadow is formed when an opaque object blocks straight light rays.

Sound Energy

Sound is a type of energy produced by vibrations, which makes us able to hear, and it travels through a medium such as air or water in waves from the source to our ears. A plucked guitar string vibrates and makes sound, clapped palms hit each other and vibrate, a drum membrane vibrates upon hitting, and our vocal cords vibrate when we talk. A vibrating ruler hanging off a desk also produces a sound that can be heard by bringing the ears close to it.

lessons.title: Force and Simple Machines: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Force is simply a push or a pull, and it can move, stop, change the speed, direction or shape of an object. Simple machines like levers, pulleys, gears and ramps make our work easier, simpler and faster.

Effects of Force on a Moving Object

Force can stop or tend to stop a moving object, for example a goal keeper stops the moving ball by catching it. Force can also change the speed of the moving object, increasing or decreasing it, for example pushing the accelerator pedal increases a car's speed and pushing the brake pedal decreases it.

Magnetic Force and Electric Force

Magnetic force is the force of attraction between a magnet and a magnetic material: a magnet sticks to an iron rod and attracts metals such as iron, nickel and cobalt. Electric force is the attraction or repulsion between two charged bodies: opposite electrically charged bodies attract each other, while like charges repel each other, for example two balloons rubbed with hair both become negatively charged and repel each other.

Friction: Advantage and Disadvantage

Advantage: friction helps us to walk and run on the ground, and we can write in a notebook and light a match stick because of friction. Disadvantage: friction reduces the efficiency of machines, and the soles of our shoes tear and the tyres of vehicles tear apart due to friction.

Lever

A lever is a simple machine that consists of a bar and rotates about a fixed point called the fulcrum: the force is applied at one end and the weight is lifted at the other end, and a lever can also change the direction of force. Examples include a sea-saw, a bottle opener and a pair of scissors.

Ramp

A ramp is a sloped plane, also called the inclined plane. Ramps help us to carry heavy loads to a height with less effort: they let us just push or pull something instead of lifting it straight up. Wheelchair ramps and sloping ramps are examples of ramps.

Uses of Friction

Friction helps us to walk and run on the ground. We can write in a notebook and on the whiteboard or blackboard because of friction, and we become able to light a match stick because of friction. The brakes of vehicles, bikes and bicycles work because of friction to slow down or stop, and knots stay tied because of friction.

Friction is a kind of resistive force that arises between any two objects in contact, it reduces the speed of objects, and it always acts in the opposite direction of motion.

Force and Its Effects

Force is simply a push or a pull: whenever you push or pull something, you use force, for example pushing a door to open it, pulling a drawer, pushing a toy car, or a train engine pulling its wagons. Force is invisible but we can feel and observe the changes due to it.

Force can make or try to make a still object move, stop or tend to stop a moving object, change the speed of a moving object, change the direction of moving objects, and change the shape or size of an object, for example the shape and size of an empty juice box changes whenever you squeeze it.

lessons.title: Classroom Project: Simple Machines in Daily Life

This is a hands-on classroom task, not a written answer.

lessons.title: Technology in Everyday Life: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Technology is the use of scientific knowledge and tools to make life better and work easier, from computers and robots to a simple pencil, hammer or nail. Scientific instruments like the thermometer, blood pressure apparatus, digital balance, stop watch and calculator help us measure, calculate and observe things precisely.

Technology

Technology is the use of scientific knowledge and tools to make the life better and work easier, or any tool or invention created for the betterment of human lives. Examples range from computers, robots and complex machines to even a pencil, hammer and simple nail, and in everyday life a mobile phone, a calculator or a thermometer are all technology.

Blood Pressure Apparatus

The blood pressure apparatus is a simple tool used widely by nurses and doctors to measure the blood pressure: it tells how hard the blood is pushing against the walls of the vein in which blood is flowing, and it is an important health monitoring tool. Its main parts are the cuff, pump, gauge and the stethoscope.

It has two types, manual and digital: the manual type is used by wrapping the cuff around the arm, inflating it and listening to the blood pulse sound with the stethoscope, while the digital type inflates and deflates the cuff itself and gives the blood pressure and heart beat reading. The normal human blood pressure reading is 120 / 80 mmHg.

Digital Devices

Nowadays there are wide varieties of available digital devices, and among these devices the mobile phones and tablets are master pieces of technology. They have a number of applications in them, such as stop watch, calculator, compass, camera and weather apps, and they are used for versatile purposes including communication, learning and knowledge.

Plumb Line

A plumb line is a very simple instrument with a piece of string and a small weight hanging with the string; the weight hanging with the string is called the plumb bob. When the plumb line is hanged down, it goes perfectly down in a straight vertical line and tells about the vertical straightness of something.

Its use is to make things stand perfectly straight and vertical, for example to install a flagpole vertically: hold the plumb line at the top of the string, bring it close to the flagpole without touching it, and adjust the flagpole until the plumb line and flagpole become perfectly parallel.

First Aid Box

Each first aid box contains band aids or plasters, antiseptic liquid or wipes, cotton, tweezers, painkillers, a first aid guide, gauze pads, adhesive tape, a pair of scissors, disposable gloves, and antiseptic cream or ointment.

Thermometer, Digital Balance and Stop Watch

A thermometer is a device used to measure the temperature; it actually tells us how hot or cold something is, and thermometers are of two types, general and clinical. It is widely used by doctors in hospitals to check if the patient has a fever or not, and it also tells us the temperature of our surroundings. The normal temperature of the human body is 37 degrees C or 98.6 degrees F.

A digital balance is a simple yet modern tool that measures the weight of objects very accurately, giving the weight in grams and kilograms, and it is widely used in shops and laboratories. Its use is very easy: just take the object you want to weigh, put it on the digital balance and it will give you the reading.

A stop watch is a simple tool used to measure time periods very accurately, with a simple stop and start button, and it helps us measure how fast an athlete can run or how long it takes to solve a math problem. Stop watches are of two types, manual and digital, both used with the start and stop button and a reset button; the manual stop watch has a clock dial and a needle that shows time, while digital stop watches show time in numbers, even telling the fractions of seconds.

lessons.title: Earth and its Resources: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Natural resources are the materials found naturally on Earth which can be used by people, like sunlight, water, soil, air, trees, minerals, animals and fossil fuels. About 71% of Earth's surface is covered with water and 29% is land, and water keeps moving between the surface and the atmosphere in the water cycle.

Natural Resources of Earth

Natural resources are the materials found naturally on Earth which can be used by people. Examples are sunlight, water (ocean, sea, river), soil, air, trees, minerals, animals and fossil fuels, and human beings use these natural resources for survival and upgrading living standards of life.

Water Bodies and Their Sources

Water bodies are the places where water is found on Earth, in the form of oceans, lakes, rivers and underground water, and three fourth of Earth's surface is covered by water. The sources of water are: oceans and seas, which are the main sources of salt water, and rivers, lakes, springs, ponds, icebergs, glaciers and underground water, which are the sources of fresh water.

Glaciers and Icebergs

Glaciers and icebergs are the frozen sources of fresh water on mountains. Glaciers are the large, massive masses of ice that are formed over the years, while the broken pieces of glaciers are icebergs. When temperature increases, glacier water flows downward towards slopy areas and reaches streams, rivers, lakes and ponds.

How Clouds are Formed

Water in oceans, rivers and lakes warms up due to heat of the Sun and evaporates in the form of invisible gas called water vapour. This water vapour rises up and turns into liquid droplets or ice crystals, a process called condensation, and a large number of these tiny droplets or ice crystals together form clouds.

Water Cycle

The water cycle is the continuous movement of water from the Earth's surface to the atmosphere and then back to the ground. It involves different weather events like cloud formation, dew formation, the evaporation of puddles, snow and rain.

Three Natural Resources in Detail

Air is a mixture of gases that surround our Earth, mostly made of nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide. Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in air, approximately 78%, that makes soil fertile for plant growth, oxygen is breathed by human beings and used by aquatic animals as dissolved oxygen, plants need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis, and oxygen in air is also used in the burning process.

Water is a vital natural resource for all living things. Three fourth of Earth's surface is covered by water, but only 3% of Earth's total water is fresh water while 97% is salt water found in oceans and seas, and fresh water is found in land water bodies like lakes, rivers, streams and glaciers.

Soil and sunlight: soil is the layer in which plant roots grow and crops and forests grow from it, and sunlight is a natural resource that warms the Earth, drives evaporation in the water cycle, and lets plants prepare their food.

Fresh Water and Salt Water

Fresh water is water that contains a low amount of salt and is suitable for drinking: only 3% of Earth's total water is fresh water, and it is found in land water bodies like lakes, rivers, streams and glaciers, and in springs, ponds, icebergs and underground water. Less than 1% of Earth's fresh water is easily accessible for human use, and most fresh water is frozen ice in glaciers or underground water.

Salt water is water that contains a large amount of dissolved salt, like sodium chloride and other minerals: 97% of total water on Earth is salt water, found in huge water bodies like oceans and seas, and this water is not suitable for human consumption, though many plants and animals rely on it for survival.

chapters.title: Unit 10: Earth in the Solar System

lessons.title: Earth in the Solar System: Main Ideas
lessons.notes_html:
Our solar system comprises the Sun, eight planets, moons, comets and asteroids, with the Sun at the center and every other celestial body revolving around it. Earth is the third nearest planet from the Sun and the only planet that provides the conditions suitable for life.

Planetary System

A planetary system is the group of planets and other heavenly bodies, such as comets, asteroids etc., revolving around the Sun. Our solar system is also an example of a planetary system.

Shadows Change Their Length

Shadows form and keep on changing during the whole day, and the formation of shadows actually proves the rotation of the Earth. In the morning, as the Sun rises from the east, the Sun is low in the sky, so the shadows formed are long and stretched in the west direction. At noon the Sun comes exactly over our heads, so the shadows formed are shorter than the whole day. After noon, as the Sun keeps on moving in the west, the shadows start to get longer and stretch again in the east.

Shadows are always formed in the opposite direction of the source of light, because light travels in straight lines and is blocked by opaque objects.

Asteroids

Asteroids are the huge or small rocks floating in space and orbiting the Sun. They have an irregular shape and are not round like planets, and they can be as big as mountains and as small as pebbles.

Day and Night

Day and night are caused by the rotation of the Earth about its own axis: Earth completes one rotation about its own axis in 24 hours. In the morning, when the Sun rises, it gives us heat and light, and in the night when the Sun sets, darkness spreads everywhere, because the part of the Earth facing the Sun has day while the part away from the Sun has night.

The Solar System

Our solar system comprises the Sun, eight planets, moons, comets, asteroids etc., and Earth is the third nearest planet from the Sun. The center of our solar system is the Sun, and every other celestial body of the solar system revolves around the Sun.

The eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, in order with respect to nearness to the Sun. The first four are called inner planets and have hard surfaces, while the last four are called the outer planets.

Our solar system has only one star, and that is the Sun, a very huge burning ball of gases and the biggest object in our solar system, placed in the center, providing all the heat and light to our Earth. The planet closest to the Sun is Mercury, and the planet closest to the Earth is Venus, and in our solar system Earth is the only planet that provides the conditions suitable for life.

Phases of the Moon

The Moon revolves around the Earth, and we see the different shapes of the Moon; sometimes it is a thin sliver and sometimes we see the full moon. The Moon completes all its phases in 29.5 days.

New Moon: during this phase, the side of the Moon facing the Sun is illuminated while the side facing the Earth is not illuminated, so in this phase we cannot see the Moon at all in the sky.

Crescent Moon: during this phase, the Moon looks like a bright thin sliver, emerging about one day after the new Moon, appearing as a faint, thin sliver of light in the sky after sunset.

Half Moon: during this phase, the Moon exactly looks like a semi-circle, appearing when the Moon travels about a quarter of its way around the Earth, and up till this point half of the Moon is illuminated by sunlight.

Full Moon: during this phase, the Moon looks like a complete bright circle, the brightest phase of the Moon, appearing once a month, approximately 15 days after a new moon.

lessons.title: Book Notes: Flags and Judgement Calls
lessons.notes_html:
This book covers all 10 units completely. The book's Glossary (p.148) and Index (p.155) are word lists with no exercises, so they carry no solved items.

Words Followed from the Book

In Unit 4, the book never uses the word xerophyte; it calls cactus a desert plant, and the book's own phrase is followed. In Unit 7, resistance and efficiency are taken verbatim from the lesson text. In Unit 9, naturally follows the book's own definition of natural resources, and soil is the unit's own answer for the layer in which plant roots grow.

Pairings and Choices Kept as Printed

In Unit 6, the loud sound and lightning pairing is the book's own column pairing: thundering is a loud sound in the lesson, and lightning is the flash that accompanies thunder. In Unit 10, the Moon is called a natural satellite, because the book states that Earth has only one natural satellite, the Moon. In Unit 8, technology makes our lives better follows the book's own introduction.

Projects, Matching Exercises and One Answer

Every unit's project is recorded as a hands-on classroom task with a short guide, not as a solved exercise, because a project has no single written answer. Each matching exercise is given as plain fact statements, because the facts themselves are what a student must learn.

In Unit 5, the needle answer applies the book's own rule: floating or sinking depends upon density; ice floats because it is less dense than water and coins sink because they are denser, so a metal needle sinks because its density is higher than water.

Book Misprints Noted

Three misprints in the printed book do not affect any answer: a sparrow is labelled among the mammals in one figure of Unit 3; one page of Unit 5 prints a wrong wording for gases where the unit's own summary gives the correct wording; and one page of Unit 7 prints maitains for maintains.
